slides.title: Get started
slides.html:

geo.title: Get started
geo.body:
Flashlight beams: two students hold flashlights at the ends of a taped segment at fixed angles. Where can the beams cross? Try to make them cross somewhere else.

  • I can explain how two matching endpoint angles force the third vertex to the same spot once the included side is matched.
  • I can tell ASA from AAS by locating the given side, and say why AAS can't be used yet.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.html: match the side, match the two rays, and two lines meet in at most one point.

geo.title: The big idea
geo.body: match the side, match the two rays, and two lines meet in at most one point.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Why ASA works (based on the ASA picture, Jacobs p. 147).

Read the worked steps
StepReason
Slide and turn triangle ABC so side AB lies on side DE.AB = DE, and rigid motions keep lengths.
If C and F are on different sides of DE, flip across DE.Now C and F are on the same side.
The angle at A matches the angle at D, so C is somewhere on ray DF.Equal angles point the same way.
The angle at B matches the angle at E, so C is also on ray EF.Same reason at the other end.
Rays DF and EF cross at only one point, F. So C lands on F.Two different lines cross at most once.
So triangle ABC ≅ triangle DEF, without SSS or the angle sum.Definition of congruence.

geo.title: Worked example
geo.prompt: Why ASA works (based on the ASA picture, Jacobs p. 147).

steps.step: Slide and turn triangle ABC so side AB lies on side DE.
steps.reason: AB = DE, and rigid motions keep lengths.

steps.step: If C and F are on different sides of DE, flip across DE.
steps.reason: Now C and F are on the same side.

steps.step: The angle at A matches the angle at D, so C is somewhere on ray DF.
steps.reason: Equal angles point the same way.

steps.step: The angle at B matches the angle at E, so C is also on ray EF.
steps.reason: Same reason at the other end.

steps.step: Rays DF and EF cross at only one point, F. So C lands on F.
steps.reason: Two different lines cross at most once.

steps.step: So triangle ABC ≅ triangle DEF, without SSS or the angle sum.

figure.alt: Why ASA works (based on the ASA picture, Jacobs p. 147).

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Two triangles sharing a side (original problem).

Read the worked steps
StepReason
C and D are on opposite sides of AB. Angle CAB ≅ angle DBA and angle CBA ≅ angle DAB.Given.
AB = BA.A segment equals itself.
AB is the side between the two marked angles in each triangle.So the side is included.
Triangle CAB ≅ triangle DBA.ASA.
CA = DB and CB = DA.Matching parts of congruent triangles (CPCTC).

slides.title: Common mistake
slides.html:
Jordan calls a non-included side ASA.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Find and fix the error

ASA and AAS put the given side in different places. Both will be valid tests, but AAS is not proved until 5.12, so you can't use it yet.

geo.title: Common mistake
geo.prompt: Jordan calls a non-included side ASA.
geo.correction: ASA and AAS put the given side in different places. Both will be valid tests, but AAS is not proved until 5.12, so you can't use it yet.

figure.alt: Jordan calls a non-included side ASA.

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
Angles A = 30 and B = 70 with side AB = 8 match angles D = 30, E = 70 and DE = 8. Which test?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

ASA.

Reveal second check

AB and DE each join the two marked corners.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
Angles A and B match angles D and E, but the matching side is AC and DF. Is that ASA?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No. The side is not between the angles. That is AAS, which we prove later.

Reveal second check

The side between angles A and B is AB.

slides.title: Practice 3
slides.html:
In Worked example 2, CA = 2x + 3 and DB = 11. Find x.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

ASA gives CA = DB, so 2x + 3 = 11 and x = 4.

Reveal second check

Plug in: 2(4) + 3 = 11.

geo.title: Practice 3
geo.prompt: In Worked example 2, CA = 2x + 3 and DB = 11. Find x.
geo.solution: ASA gives CA = DB, so 2x + 3 = 11 and x = 4.

figure.alt: In Worked example 2, CA = 2x + 3 and DB = 11. Find x.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.html:
In the ASA argument, why does C have to land exactly on F?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

C lies on both ray DF and ray EF, and two rays that are not on the same line meet in at most one point, which is F.

Reveal second check

Name the givens and the theorem or definition used.
